spine.promotion_rule: operator review -> author full conscience fields (detection pair, blast_radius, reversibility, requires_confirmation) -> move to techniques/*.json

techniques.name: IAM Privilege Escalation Paths
techniques.summary: AWS-style graphs of forgotten permissions: iam:PassRole + a compute action (run a workload with any role), iam:CreateAccessKey on another user, sts:AssumeRole chains, lambda:UpdateFunctionCode to hijack a privileged function. Rhino's research made these paths computable; Pacu automates them; cloudgoat teaches them hands-on.

detection.description: CloudTrail: CreateAccessKey/CreatePolicyVersion/AssumeRole anomalies per principal, PassRole on unusual compute launches, role assumptions from novel ASNs/regions, GuardDuty privilege-escalation findings, Config drift on IAM policy.
mitigations: Least-privilege IAM with periodic review (IAM Access Analyzer)
Permissions-boundary on every role; deny iam:CreateAccessKey broadly
SCPs blocking high-risk IAM actions outside break-glass roles
CloudTrail enabled org-wide, alerting on the Rhino escalation primitives

techniques.name: Metadata Credential Theft (IMDS Abuse)
techniques.summary: Any code execution on an instance plus SSRF reaches the metadata service and walks away with role credentials - the Capital One breach in one move. IMDSv2 (token via PUT, hop-limit 1) closes the SSRF path; plain IMDSv1 remains open on fleets that never got the memo.

detection.description: VPC flow logs to 169.254.169.254 from non-instance paths, GuardDuty SSRF/ec2 metadata findings, unusual GetRole/GetCredentials on instance profiles, AssumeRole events immediately following app-tier anomalies.
mitigations: IMDSv2 required (HttpTokens=required, hop-limit 1) - fleet-wide, enforced by SCP
Egress filtering from app tier
Instance-role scope minimal; no admin roles on internet-facing workloads
Short-lived credentials + automatic rotation

techniques.name: Container Escape & K8s RBAC Abuse
techniques.summary: Break the boundary: privileged containers (fd access to host devices), hostPath mounts, docker.sock exposure (docker-in-docker is root on the host), kernel primitives, or K8s RBAC paths (pod-create with a privileged spec, service-account token theft, exec into high-priv pods). The crown-jewel jump is always node-level.

detection.description: K8s audit logs: pod-create with privileged/hostPath specs, exec into sensitive namespaces, SA token use from novel IPs; container runtime anomalies (mount of host paths, namespace transitions), eBPF-based runtime security (Falco rules for container breakout patterns).
mitigations: Pod Security Standards (restricted profile), no privileged pods without exception registry
No docker.sock mounts; rootless containers where feasible; seccomp/AppArmor defaults
Least-privilege RBAC per namespace; no default-SA automount for unprivileged workloads
Runtime security (Falco/Tetragon) for syscall-level breakout detection

techniques.name: Serverless & Event-Driven Abuse
techniques.summary: Function code with injection classes (event payloads are user input: S3 keys, headers, queue messages), oversized-bill DoS (recursion, fan-out amplification), event-data poisoning that lands in downstream sinks (the 'serverless SQLi'), and cross-function trust abuse via unwritten event schemas.

detection.description: Function error-rate and invocation anomalies, concurrency spikes near account limits, CloudTrail PutBucketPolicy/CreateAccessKey from function roles, unusual egress from function VPCs, downstream data-store query anomalies correlating with event sources.
mitigations: Treat every event field as untrusted input (validate schemas strictly)
Function-role least privilege; no wildcard actions on data planes
Concurrency caps + budget alerts (the DoS answer is financial, not technical)
Recursion guards and dead-letter queues with alerting

techniques.name: Process Injection (Hollowing / APC / Thread Hijack)
techniques.summary: Write code into another process's memory and execute it there: hollow a legitimate process's image (replace entry content), queue APC to an alertable thread, or hijack thread context. Runs under a trusted binary's identity - the classic pairing with every initial-access payload.

detection.description: Cross-process memory writes (Sysmon EID 8/10, EDR); RWX private regions in unexpected processes; svchost/notepad with writable executable memory; thread start addresses outside the loaded image; parent-child anomalies.
mitigations: EDR behavioral coverage (injection telemetry beats signature), Sysmon EID 8/10 baseline
CFG / XFG, arbitrary code guard on browsers
Block credential-theft-relevant processes from injection via exploit protection

techniques.name: AMSI Bypass
techniques.summary: Patch the amsi!AmsiScanBuffer return value or the provider's_dll!_CanLoad branch so script content is scanned-and-forgiven. Standard prelude to any PowerShell/JS tradecraft; every red team course teaches the current variant. Short lifecycle per bypass - each known patch gets blocked and a new one is found.

detection.description: Access to amsi.dll memory from managed processes (ETW), EDR hooks on VirtualProtect targeting amsi.dll, PowerShell transcription logging surviving (bypass does not disable transcription), module-unhook signals; block known patch byte-patterns at EDR.
mitigations: PowerShell Constrained Language Mode + transcription + script-block logging (all three)
EDR/AMSI tamper telemetry (patch attempts are themselves high-signal)
Latest .NET/AMSI updates; don't rely on AMSI alone as a control

techniques.name: ETW Patching & Log Tampering
techniques.summary: Patch the EtwEventWrite provider registration or clear logs (wevtutil cl, audit policy flips, timestomping with $FILE_NAME vs $STANDARD_INFORMATION mismatch). Blinding telemetry is the tell that the operator expects to do worse things next - treat as force-multiplier alert, not noise.

detection.description: EtwEventWrite patch attempts (EDR kernel callbacks), log-clear EIDs (1102, 104), audit policy change EIDs (4719), timestomping detection ($SI/$FN delta via NTFS analysis), service/telemetry process termination by unexpected callers.
mitigations: Forward logs off-host in near-real-time (the only real answer to local clearing)
Tamper-protected EDR (self-protection), protected event log (RFC 5849-style wrapping)
Alert on any 1102/104/4719 - these should be rare organizational events

techniques.name: Direct Syscalls & Unhooking (ntdll Refresh)
techniques.summary: Skip hooked user-land APIs entirely: resolve syscall numbers (SSN) from a clean ntdll copy (mapped fresh from disk or the KnownDlls section) or via Hell's Gate/Halo's Gate, then issue syscalls directly - EDR user-mode hooks never see the traffic. This is the modern baseline for offensive tooling and the reason userland hooking alone is not a defense.

detection.description: Kernel-side telemetry is the counter: ETW Ti provider, minifilter file events, syscall anomalies (direct syscalls still hit kernel callbacks), memory regions with RWX and executable syscalls, indirect-syscall stack-spoofing artifacts (return address outside loaded images).
mitigations: Assume userland hooks fail; invest in kernel telemetry + behavioral analytics
Call-stack analysis for return addresses outside known images
Flow-based rather than API-based detections (e.g. 'a process read LSASS memory', regardless of API used)

techniques.name: Living Off the Land (Signed Binary Proxy Execution)
techniques.summary: Abuse signed native tools as proxies: rundll32 executing export ordinals, mshta rendering remote HTA, regsvr32 /i:http, InstallUtil, msbuild inline-task builds, bitsadmin/certutil for transfer. No malware on disk - the LOLBins are the malware, and LOLBas/GTFOBins catalog them exhaustively.

detection.description: Command-line analytics (Sysmon EID 1): office/document apps spawning LOLBins, LOLBins with network URLs in arguments, rundll32 without .dll arguments, mshta spawning children; netconn anomalies (EID 3) from binaries that never legitimately call out.
mitigations: Block LOLB in document/browser context via ASR rules
WDAC allowlisting makes unsigned-argument abuse moot on hardened fleets
Command-line audit + Sigma coverage on the standard abuse arguments

techniques.name: Stack Buffer Overflow to Control Flow Hijack
techniques.summary: Overwrite a stack-resident buffer past its boundary to control the instruction pointer, then redirect execution (ret2libc / ROP when NX is present). A crash under attacker-controlled input is the classic tell that this class is present.

detection.description: Repeated process crashes with access violations at identical offsets; WER/appcrash logs; canary mismatch reports; abnormally long argument buffers against a service input; SIGSEGV correlation with input length.
mitigations: Compile with stack canaries (/GS, -fstack-protector-strong)
ASLR + DEP/NX enforced fleet-wide
Control Flow Guard / Shadow Stack on new builds
Input length validation and fuzzing (AFL++, libFuzzer) in CI

techniques.name: Heap Exploitation (Use-After-Free / Allocator Abuse)
techniques.summary: The classic memory-corruption family against dynamic allocation: corrupt heap metadata or reuse freed objects (UAF, double-free, tcache poisoning in glibc) to gain an arbitrary write or object confusion primitive, then escalate to code execution. Allocator versions matter enormously; modern hardening (safe-linking) changed the playbook.

detection.description: Heap corruption aborts (glibc 'double free or corruption'), AddressSanitizer findings, native crash reports with heap-corruption buckets, anomaly spikes in freed-object reuse paths.
mitigations: Sanitizer coverage (ASan/UBSan) in CI for native code
Allocator hardening: hardened_malloc, glibc safe-linking, Windows Segment Heap
Rust/managed languages for components handling untrusted input

techniques.name: Format String Abuse
techniques.summary: Pass attacker-controlled format specifiers (%n, %p) into printf-style functions to leak memory (defeat ASLR) or write arbitrary values (the %n primitive). Rare in fresh code but endemic in legacy C services and logging paths.

detection.description: Input validation should reject '%' sequences in logged strings; runtime detection via format-attribute compiler warnings (-Wformat-security); IDS strings for '%n' in network inputs to C services.
mitigations: Never pass user data as the format string (use printf('%s', data))
Compile with -Wformat -Wformat-security -Werror=format-security
Fuzz log-path and message-path inputs

techniques.name: Race Conditions / TOCTOU Privilege Escalation
techniques.summary: Win a timing window between a privileged check and a privileged use (symlink swaps, file descriptor races, signal handlers, double-spends in payment logic). Non-deterministic by nature: reliability comes from retry loops, which are themselves a detection signal.

detection.description: High-frequency rename/open/unlink patterns against protected paths from a single principal; audit logs showing check-then-use pairs executing out of order; anomalous retry volume (the same request thousands of times).
mitigations: Open fds / O_NOFOLLOW / mandatory locking instead of path-based re-checks
Atomic primitives and per-session idempotency keys
Rate-limit and alert on retry storms

techniques.name: Client-Side Exploitation (Document & Browser Based)
techniques.summary: Weaponize document parsers (Office, PDF) or browser engines against user workstations: malformed structures trigger the parser bug, shellcode stages the payload. In engagements this is the standard pairing with phishing (the user is the exploit delivery mechanism).

detection.description: Office/PDF spawning child processes (Winword.exe -> cmd.exe is nearly always hostile), office products writing .exe/.scr, EDR behavioral rules on macro-to-shell lineage, crash telemetry at identical frames across hosts.
mitigations: Attack Surface Reduction rules (block Office child processes, Win32 API from macro)
Patching cadence for browsers and document suites
Mark-of-the-Web enforcement, macro-block-by-default policy
Phishing-resistant user training plus report-button workflow

techniques.name: Kerberoasting
techniques.summary: Request service tickets (TGS) for accounts with SPNs; the ticket is encrypted with the service account's NTLM hash, so it can be cracked offline at leisure. No admin rights needed to request tickets - any domain user can enumerate and roast. Weak service-account passwords fall in minutes.

detection.description: Windows EID 4769 with RC4 (0x17) encryption and no 4768 in the same session; abnormal volume of TGS requests from a single principal in a short window; RC4 tickets are themselves legacy-flagged.
mitigations: 25+ character random passwords on all service accounts, or gMSA (group Managed Service Accounts)
Disable RC4 where possible; enforce AES
Alert on 4769 RC4 request bursts; tiered admin model keeps service accounts out of Domain Admins

techniques.name: AS-REP Roasting
techniques.summary: Accounts with 'Do not require Kerberos preauthentication' return an AS-REP encrypted with the user's own key to anyone who asks - offline crackable, no credentials needed at all. The misconfiguration is older-domain legacy and quiet, so enumeration finds surprises.

detection.description: EID 4768 with pre-auth type 0 (no preauth); volume of AS requests against accounts that normally never authenticate interactively; hashcat-mode 18200 activity indicators from EDR on endpoints.
mitigations: Audit and clear the UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH flag - it should be false on every account
Strong passphrases / gMSA as backstop
Alert on 4768 preauth-missing events

techniques.name: Pass-the-Hash / Pass-the-Ticket
techniques.summary: Replay stolen credential material without ever knowing the password: NTLM hash passed directly to authentication, or a captured Kerberos ticket injected into a new session. Lateral movement with zero credential cracking - the reason credential theft beats password attacks in real engagements.

detection.description: EID 4624 logon type 3 (network) with NTLM where host normally uses Kerberos; ticket reuse across hosts within a ticket lifetime (same logon ID, different source machines); abnormal NTLM traffic between workstations (workstation-to-workstation NTLM is nearly always lateral movement).
mitigations: Credential Guard (isolates LSASS secrets via virtualization)
Tiered admin model - admin credentials never touch non-tier-0 hosts
Restricted Admin Mode / Remote Credential Guard for RDP
Disable NTLM where feasible; else NTLM auditing and SMB signing

techniques.name: DCSync Replication Abuse
techniques.summary: Hold 'Replicating Directory Changes' rights (or steal a DC's trust) and ask a domain controller to replicate password hashes directly - every account in the domain, including krbtgt. The endgame move: with krbtgt's hash you forge golden tickets. Treat as game-over, not a checkpoint.

detection.description: EID 4662 'Replicating Directory Changes' access by non-DC principals; replication attempts to member workstations; Get-ReplicationChanges API calls from unexpected sources. DC-to-workstation replication is a definitive alert.
mitigations: Audit 'Replicating Directory Changes' ACEs - only DCs and sanctioned tools should hold them
Tier 0 isolation for DCs (no interactive logon by non-DC admins)
After compromise: krbtgt password reset TWICE (the interval rule) - and plan for it in IR

techniques.name: Golden / Silver Ticket Forgery
techniques.summary: With krbtgt's NTLM hash, mint offline-valid TGTs for any identity, any group, ten-year lifetime - golden tickets that outlive the compromise that created them. Silver tickets (service-account hash) forge TGS for one service with no DC contact at all, making them quieter and harder to correlate.

detection.description: Ticket anomalies: lifetime violations, missing PAC, or PAC signature mismatches; EID 4769 requests for services with no prior 4768 TGT issuance; tickets referencing accounts with no corresponding domain activity. Full detection is hard - the durability of the artifact is the point.
mitigations: Protect krbtgt hash: tier-0 hygiene, DCSync defense, dual krbtgt password rotation post-incident
Restrict service-account privilege; any account whose hash is stolen silvers only that one service
PAC signature validation and ticket-lifetime anomaly tooling (e.g. defcon/BlueHive-class log analysis)

techniques.name: NTLM Relay (incl. ESC8 Web Enrollment)
techniques.summary: Relay an authenticated NTLM handshake to another service that accepts it: coerce a machine to authenticate to the attacker (Printerbug, PetitPotam) and forward to LDAP/SMB/AD-CS web enrollment. Signing/sealing (SMB, LDAP) blocks it; plain HTTP endpoints (AD CS CertSrv) do not, which is why ESC8 became the modern kill chain's favorite door.

detection.description: Coercion indicators: machine-triggered authentication to unusual hosts (EID 4625/4776 correlation, MS-EFSR/MS-RPRN calls logged via Sysmon EID 3 to non-standard destinations); relay signatures: NTLM auth to ADCS/LDAP from a workstation address that should never do so.
mitigations: Enable SMB and LDAP signing/sealing everywhere (the fundamental fix)
Disable NTLM entirely or restrict to explicit allowlist; disable ADCS HTTP enrollment or require Kerberos/EPA
Patch coercion vectors (PetitPotam fix) and disable Print Spooler on servers not needing it
Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) on AD CS

techniques.name: AD CS Misconfiguration Abuse (ESC1-ESC8)
techniques.summary: Certificate templates misconfigured (ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT, low-ACL enrollment, manager-approval gaps, HTTP-only enrollment) let any domain user mint certificates impersonating privileged principals - authentication that bypasses password policy entirely and leaves no NTLM/LM artifacts.

detection.description: Certification Authority audit (EID 4887/4899) showing enrollment for privileged templates from non-privileged callers; issued certificates with SAN mismatches; Certipy/Locksmith-style audit tooling run on a schedule is itself the primary defense because detection in-flight is weak.
mitigations: Run Locksmith / PSPKIAudit - remediate template ACLs and flag settings (ESC1-8 checklist is now a standard hardening task)
Disable ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT unless a template truly requires it
Enforce manager approval + authorized signatures on high-privilege templates
Kill HTTP enrollment (EPA required) - closes ESC8 and the relay kill chain together

techniques.name: ACL & Delegation Abuse (BloodHound Paths)
techniques.summary: Enterprise AD is a graph of forgotten permissions: GenericAll on a user (shadow credential / target kerberoast), WriteDacl on a group, DCSync rights on an OU, unconstrained or resource-based constrained delegation letting a machine impersonate anyone to a target service. BloodHound made these paths computable - which cuts both ways, and the defensive use is the same tool.

detection.description: EID 5136 (directory object changes) on privileged objects; new SPNs set on accounts (delegation staging); certificate-based shadow-credential activity (EID 4887 msDS-KeyCredentialLink writes);BloodHound collection itself is visible - SharpHound sessions from non-audit hosts should alert.
mitigations: BloodHound run defensively on a schedule - find your own attack paths before they do
Strip unsanctioned ACEs from tier-0 objects; tiered admin model
Restrict delegation: no unconstrained delegation outside cluster needs, RBCD scoping documented
EID 5136 auditing on privileged containers

techniques.name: Password Spraying & Credential Stuffing
techniques.summary: The anti-pattern of brute force: one or two very common passwords rotated across many usernames (spraying), or replaying breach-corpus credential pairs (stuffing). Auth failures blend into baseline noise, so the move trades loudness per account for breadth across accounts - which is also exactly the shape defenders hunt for. Noisy-but-recoverable by doctrine; the blast lands as account lockouts and alert fatigue.

detection.description: Breadth-over-rate heuristic: single source IP/session generating EID 4625/4771 failures across MANY distinct accounts is spraying, even at low rate; lockout spikes (EID 4740) cluster downstream; Entra ID sign-in risk detections and breach-password match telemetry flag stuffing at cloud IdPs; watch for distributed-source sprays via fail2ban-style correlation and geovelocity anomalies.
mitigations: Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2) - renders stolen passwords inert
Smart lockout that splits per-user and per-source thresholds (avoids the lockout-DoS side effect)
Breached-password screening and deny-lists at password change, not just login
Conditional access with device compliance for legacy-protocol exemptions kept to zero

techniques.name: SQL Injection (Union / Error Based)
techniques.summary: Craft input that terminates a string context and appends attacker SQL: union-select to exfiltrate arbitrary tables, error-based to read data through verbose database errors. Full read/write against the database backend, sometimes to RCE via sp_execute/INTO OUTFILE.

detection.description: WAF/IDS patterns for quote-terminators plus SQL keywords in parameters; anomalous 500s and database error text in responses; sudden large row-count queries from application service accounts; SELECT volume on tables the app never reads in normal flow.
mitigations: Parameterized queries / prepared statements everywhere (the actual fix)
ORM query APIs with bound parameters; never string-concatenate SQL
Least-privilege DB accounts per service; disable dangerous features (xp_cmdshell, FILE)
Generic error pages; never echo SQL error detail to clients

techniques.name: Blind SQL Injection (Boolean / Time / Out-of-Band)
techniques.summary: Extract data one bit at a time when output is not reflected: conditionals flip page content (boolean), sleep/CASE delays encode bits (time), or DNS/HTTP callbacks exfiltrate the answer (OOB). Slow, noisy in aggregate, and the most common path when error-based is suppressed.

detection.description: Request-pattern analytics: same endpoint with systematically varied parameter values, stable inter-request timing, per-character enumeration velocity; DB audit logs showing repeated information_schema queries; out-of-band DNS lookups from the DB host (the smoking gun for OOB).
mitigations: Same parameterization fix as reflected SQLi
Rate-limit and fingerprint repetitive enumeration (queries per second per session)
Egress filtering from database hosts (blocks OOB channels entirely)

techniques.name: OS Command Injection
techniques.summary: Application shells out to a system binary with user-controlled arguments; metacharacters (; | && $()) break out into arbitrary command execution under the web service account. Direct route to RCE with almost no specialized tooling required.

detection.description: Web server accounts spawning shells or binaries they never legitimately run; process ancestry violations (nginx/apache -> bash, w3wp -> cmd.exe); egress attempts immediately following parameterized requests; WAF metacharacter alerts.
mitigations: Never invoke shells from web code; use language-native libraries and strict allowlists
If unavoidable: argv-array execution, no shell, strict input allowlisting (regex ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$)
Run workers under least-privilege, no-shell-required service identities
Process-ancestry monitoring (Sysmon EID 1, Linux auditd execve) alerting on lineage breaks

techniques.name: Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI)
techniques.summary: User input embedded into a template before rendering: template syntax like {{7*7}} or ${7*7} evaluates server-side, and in engines such as Jinja2/Twig/Freemarker the object graph leads to process execution (SSTI is usually RCE in an evening of work). Fingerprint the engine first, then walk its sandbox escapes.

detection.description: Responses reflecting arithmetic payloads evaluated server-side (49 instead of {{7*7}}); template engine exceptions in logs referencing user strings; process spawn under template/cache directories; poll-based WAF alerts for ${} and {{}}.
mitigations: Treat templates as code: never render user input as template source, pass it as context data
Sandboxed engines with restricted globals, deny-list of dunder/attribute chains
Alert on template-engine stack traces containing request data

techniques.name: XML External Entity Injection (XXE)
techniques.summary: If the XML parser resolves external entities, DOCTYPE definitions read local files (file://), pivot to internal services (http:// - the SSRF bridge), or exfiltrate out-of-band via parameter entities. Legacy SOAP endpoints and anything accepting XML file uploads are prime surface.

detection.description: DOCTYPE/ENTITY keywords in request bodies at WAF; local file paths appearing in application errors; XML parser library stack traces; outbound requests from the application host to internal-only addresses immediately after XML uploads.
mitigations: Disable DTDs and external entities at the parser (disallow-doctype-decl, ENTITY false) - the complete fix
Prefer JSON; where XML remains, use SAX/StAX with features locked down
Egress filtering from app tier to internal service ranges

techniques.name: Insecure Deserialization
techniques.summary: Deserializing attacker-controlled objects (Java serialized streams, .NET ViewState, PHP objects, Python pickle) instantiates gadget chains that end in code execution. ViewState without MAC validation, pre-auth Java gadget chains (Commons-Collections class), and pickle in web apps are the canonical instances.

detection.description: Serialized-object signatures in request bodies (rO0A, O:x, aca26d for .NET ViewState); ysoserial-pattern payloads at WAF; gadget-class names (InvokerTransformer, ObjectInputStream) in stack traces; heap-dump review after anomalies.
mitigations: Never deserialize untrusted data with native object formats; use JSON with strict schemas
ViewState: enforce MAC validation and latest encryption (machineKey hygiene)
Upgrade gadget-bearing libraries; monitor deserialization exceptions
RASP/runtime hooks on ObjectInputStream-style entry points for high-risk apps

techniques.name: ARP Spoofing / MITM Positioning
techniques.summary: Flood gratuitous ARP replies mapping the gateway's IP to your MAC; hosts send their traffic to you first. Combined with port mirroring or SSL stripping it becomes full credential capture. Purely local-segment scope, trivially detected, still effective on unmanaged networks.

detection.description: MAC-flapping on switch ports (same MAC bouncing across ports), gratuitous-ARP rate anomalies, duplicate IP alarms, gateway IP resolving to non-gateway MAC in host caches; DHCP starvation usually accompanies it.
mitigations: Dynamic ARP Inspection + DHCP snooping on switches (the actual fix)
Static ARP entries for critical infrastructure pairs
802.1X to keep rogue devices off the segment
TLS everywhere - MITM position without TLS stripping is mostly metadata

techniques.name: DNS Poisoning & Spoofing
techniques.summary: Inject forged DNS responses: on-path guessing with transaction-ID prediction (Kaminsky-class cache poisoning), rogue DHCP DNS assignment, or local hosts manipulation. Redirects everything downstream - which is why DNSSEC and port randomization exist.

detection.description: Resolver analytics: unusual response source ports/addresses, TTL anomalies on popular records, NXDOMAIN bursts (subdomain enumeration is noisy in the same logs), organic lookup volume to unregistered domains via a single host.
mitigations: DNSSEC validation on resolvers
Source-port + query-ID randomization (modern resolvers have it; audit old ones)
Split-horizon hygiene: internal resolvers forward only to trusted upstreams
Monitor for DHCP options 6 changes

techniques.name: TCP Session Hijacking & RST Attacks
techniques.summary: On-path sequence-number tracking lets you inject into an established stream (desync then command injection) or send forged RSTs to kill connections (IDS evasion, VoIP/long-session disruption). Mostly a LAN or compromised-router technique in modern practice.

detection.description: TCP retransmission/ACK anomalies per flow (IDES-class heuristics), unexpected RST storms between specific pairs, session resumption from different source IPs, out-of-window segment counters on stateful devices.
mitigations: Encrypted, integrity-checked sessions (TLS 1.3) - injected bytes die at the MAC check
TCP-AO for routing/infrastructure sessions
Stateful inspection devices flag out-of-window traffic

techniques.name: BGP Hijacking & Route Manipulation
techniques.summary: Announce prefixes you don't own (origin hijack) or a more-specific path (path poisoning) to attract traffic for interception or blackout. Nation-state tier: nation-states and large ASes have executed it for interception (documented incidents exist). Affects the whole internet's view, not one network.

detection.description: Route monitoring (RIPE RIS, RouteViews) for origin/AS-path anomalies on your prefixes, sudden geolocation shifts of inbound source, RPKI-invalid announcements, certificate pinning failures reported by clients (passive DNS + RPKI dashboards are the operational answer).
mitigations: RPKI ROA publication for every prefix (origin validation)
ASPA (path validation) as it deploys, max-prefix limits with peers
IRR + RPKI hygiene, IRR filtering discipline on your edge
Certificate pinning in clients for crown-jewel apps (interception becomes visible)

techniques.name: LLMNR/NBT-NS/mDNS Poisoning (Responder-class)
techniques.summary: Answer Windows name-resolution fallback queries (typo'd hostnames, WPAD lookups) claiming to be anything, capturing NetNTLMv1/v2 hashes from the victims. The classic first 20 minutes of an internal engagement - capture, crack offline, or relay upstream (welds directly to the NTLM relay technique).

detection.description: Multiple hosts answering LLMNR/NBT-NS queries (legitimate: zero extra responders), WPAD resolution anomalies, EID 4625/4776 auth bursts to a single host after name queries, RDP/HTTP auth attempts to hosts with no service.
mitigations: Disable LLMNR/NBT-NS via GPO (the actual fix; no legitimate modern need)
Disable WPAD; DNS globally suffices
SMB signing everywhere (blocks the relay half)
Network IDS signatures for responder traffic patterns

techniques.name: Host & Service Discovery (Network Scanning)
techniques.summary: The first move of nearly every real engagement: ICMP sweeps, ARP discovery on the local segment, SYN/connect scans for listening services, version fingerprints to pick targets. Read-class by nature - but scanning is NOT harmless: known-naive connect scans have hard-crashed printers, OT/ICS gear, and fragile legacy services, so scope and rate discipline are operational safety, not courtesy. Outside the engagement scope a scan is indistinguishable from pre-attack recon, which is the whole reason defenders instrument for it.

detection.description: Shape, not signature: one source touching many ports on one host, or many hosts on one port - both are scan shapes visible in Zeek/Suricata scan detectors and firewall deny spikes; Windows sides show EID 5156 connect-storm patterns; honeypot canaries (unused RFC1918 space, decoy services) give certain-signal alerts; sudden DNS/ARP sweep traffic marks host-discovery phases; asset-inventory diffs flag services that appear where none were.
mitigations: Deny-by-default east-west segmentation - shrink what any scan can even see
Canary nets and decoy hosts on every segment; any touch is a high-fidelity alert
NAC (802.1X) so only managed endpoints get a routable identity
Baseline inventory + anomaly alerting on new listening services

techniques.name: Kernel / OS-Level LPE Exploits
techniques.summary: Public kernel exploits (PrintNightmare-class, Dirty Pipe, catch-all driver primitives) turn user-land footholds into SYSTEM/root. The reliability game is patch-level fingerprinting: knowing which kernel build is vulnerable before firing anything.

detection.description: Kernel driver load events from user paths (Sysmon EID 6), suspicious named-pipe activity around spooler/services, process token changes, EDR alerts on known exploit tooling signatures (Printspoofer, etc.).
mitigations: Patch cadence - the real fix
Unprivileged driver load blocking, Microsoft Vulnerable Driver Blocklist
Restrict Spooler service on non-print servers
Credential Guard and VBS raise the floor

techniques.name: Service Misconfiguration Escalation (Path, ACL, Unquoted)
techniques.summary: Services running as SYSTEM with: unquoted binary paths (C:\Program Files\Vendor\svc.exe hijacks to C:\Program.exe), weak ACLs on the service or its binary (ChangeServiceConfig via accesschk), or world-writable directories in the DLL search order. Enumeration is cheap; the misconfigurations are endemic.

detection.description: Service binary path writes by non-SYSTEM principals (Sysmon EID 11 on service directories), service reconfiguration events (EID 7045/4697), accesschk/BeClass-class enumeration tooling process starts.
mitigations: Quote every service binary path (deployment lint rule)
icacls audit on service directories; ACL should be SYSTEM/Administrators write-only
Monitor EID 7045 for new service installs by non-admins

techniques.name: Token Impersonation & UAC Bypass
techniques.summary: Steal or impersonate primary/impersonation tokens of privileged processes (SeImpersonate abuse via Potato-class token coercion, or named-pipe token capture), and abuse auto-elevate binaries (fodhelper, computerdefaults) to skip the UAC prompt when in a high-integrity-eligible context.

detection.description: Named-pipe creation by unusual processes, token privilege assignments (EID 4673), auto-elevate binary spawning with command-line arguments pointing to temp (Sysmon EID 1 lineage: fodhelper.exe -> cmd.exe), potato-class tool signatures.
mitigations: Remove SeImpersonatePrivilege from service accounts that don't need it
UAC set to 'Always Notify' (blocks most auto-elevate abuse)
EDR lineage rules on auto-elevate binaries
Credential Guard, and patch Potato-class vectors (they ride legitimate DCOM/RPC behaviors)

techniques.name: DLL Search Order Hijacking & Side-Loading
techniques.summary: Plant a malicious DLL in a directory searched before the legitimate one, or proxy a legitimate signed binary's imports (side-load via version.dll, winmm.dll in a known-vulnerable signed app). The signed-binary variant doubles as defense evasion, which is why it survives so long in the wild.

detection.description: Sysmon EID 7 (image load) - DLLs loaded from user-writable paths, unsigned DLLs loaded by signed processes, new DLL writes into application directories (EID 11); known-abused binaries appearing in odd contexts.
mitigations: Set DLL directory to absolute, use SetDefaultDllDirectories where possible
Code-signing requirement on loaded modules for high-value apps
ACL application directories to admin-write-only
EDR image-load rules for user-path loads by privileged processes

techniques.name: Linux SUID / Capabilities / Cron / PATH Abuse
techniques.summary: The classic Unix ladder: SUID binaries with shell escapes (GTFOBins is literally a lookup table), file capabilities (cap_setuid on an interpreter), world-writable cron scripts, PATH shadowing in root-invoked scripts, and sudo rules with NOPASSWD on interpreters or wildcards.

detection.description: auditd execve with euid=0 from unexpected binaries; new SUID binaries appearing (file integrity monitoring, e.g. AIDE); cron edits by non-root; sudo invocations with unusual arguments (sudoers EID-logging via sudoers audit plugin).
mitigations: File integrity monitoring for SUID drift; scheduled SUID inventory diffs
sudo: NOEXEC/arg restriction, no NOPASSWD on interpreters, secure_path enforced
Cron scripts: absolute paths, root-owned directories, chattr on stable scripts
Remove file capabilities not required at runtime (getcap -r / sweep)

techniques.name: Phishing & Spear Phishing Infrastructure
techniques.summary: Weaponized email: credential-harvest clones, macro documents, link-t0-evil-twin-portal chains. The infrastructure game (lookalike domains, SPF/DKIM/DMARC pass-through via lookalikes, MFA-aware reverse proxies like Evilginx-class tooling that proxy the real login and steal the session cookie) is what separates spray-and-pray from targeted compromise.

detection.description: Lookalike-domain registrations (dnstwist-class monitoring as defense), impossible-travel logins, session-cookie replay from novel ASNs (the reverse-proxy tell), mailbox-rule creation post-login, report-button volume as the human sensor.
mitigations: Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/WebAuthn) - session theft dies here (proxied logins get useless)
DMARC enforcement (p=reject) + lookalike-domain monitoring
User report-button culture with fast feedback loops
Conditional access: device compliance + location heuristics

techniques.name: Vishing, MFA Fatigue & Helpdesk Social Engineering
techniques.summary: Voice-first compromise: MFA-push spam until approval (fatigue), helpdesk password resets against a confident voice with a name and employee-adjacent details (the MGM-class pattern), SIM-swap to own SMS-based MFA. The 2023 casino breaches made this the textbook modern initial access.

detection.description: MFA push denial-rate spikes per user (denials are telemetry: report the fatigue attempt), repeated reset requests per identity, helpdesk verification failures in tickets, SIM-swap indicators (carrier alerts, sudden SMS silence followed by failed logins).
mitigations: Number matching in MFA push (kills blind-approve fatigue)
Helpdesk verification: manager + ticket + video or identity-proofing for resets - zero voice-only resets for privileged accounts
FIDO2 over push/SMS wherever possible; carrier-level SIM-swap locks
Log and alert every MFA denial

techniques.name: Pretexting & Physical Intrusion (Tailgating, Badge Cloning)
techniques.summary: Physical access is root access: tailgating behind badge holders, cloned HID-seucer credentials (the classic low-frequency 125 kHz cards clone with a $30 device), delivery-person pretexts, conference-room installs. Once inside: network drops in conference rooms, posted passwords, unattended laptops.

detection.description: Badge-in without badge-out pairs, door-forced-open alarms, anti-passback violations, camera-review flags (no visible human at badge events), unknown MACs on internal drops, physical access anomalies correlated with logical anomalies.
mitigations: Mantrap entries, security-desk badge verification, anti-passback enforcement
Upgrade to high-frequency smart credentials (SEOS-class) or mobile credentials
Network-drop 802.1X (a plugged-in cable is not access)
Clean-desk policy, screen-lock enforcement, visitor escort culture

techniques.name: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
techniques.summary: Make the server issue requests of your choosing: hit cloud metadata (169.254.169.254 - instant IAM credentials), pivot into internal-only services, scan the RFC1918 space from inside. The cloud-era killer because the metadata endpoint hands over role credentials to anyone who can make the host talk to itself.

detection.description: Egress logs from app tier to link-local/metadata addresses, DNS for internal hostnames initiated by app processes, unusual URL schemes in request parameters (file://, gopher://), WAF rules for metadata IPs, canary tokens on metadata endpoints.
mitigations: IMDSv2 (token-required, hop-limit) on all cloud instances - the definitive metadata fix
Egress allowlists from app tier (default deny to RFC1918 + link-local)
URL validation against allowlist schemes/hosts; never accept raw URLs from users
Separate network zones so app compromise does not equal internal reach

techniques.name: Path Traversal & Local File Inclusion
techniques.summary: Read (and sometimes execute) arbitrary files by walking out of a sanitized path: ../../../etc/passwd, encoded variants (%2e%2e%2f), PHP filters (php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=index), null bytes in legacy parsers. LFI plus log poisoning or session files crosses into RCE.

detection.description: WAF traversal-pattern rules, application errors revealing file paths, anomalous access to /etc/, win.ini, web.config from app logs, high volume of 200s on deep-dot segments, php:// filter strings in access logs.
mitigations: Never build paths from user input - map IDs to fixed paths server-side (the real fix)
Chroot/containerize file access for the app user
Deny-list directories at the web server layer as a second wall
Least-privilege service accounts (can't read what the account can't read)

techniques.name: Authentication & Session Logic Abuse
techniques.summary: The soft, high-yield class: broken session validation (predictable tokens, missing rotation on privilege change), mass assignment to role fields, JWT alg=none/key confusion, reset-link enumeration, 2FA logic gaps (response manipulation, brute-forceable OTP windows, missing step-up). Rarely toolable - it is reasoning work, which is exactly why it survives.

detection.description: Login-success anomalies per account (impossible-travel, new-ASN), session token reuse across IPs, JWT validation errors in app logs, password-reset bursts against one account from distributed sources, 2FA-step error-rate anomalies.
mitigations: Framework auth (battle-tested) over hand-rolled; deny-by-default route guards
Session rotation on login AND privilege change; short lifetimes; secure flags
JWT: strict alg allowlist, aud/iss validation, short exp
Rate-limit and alert on reset flows; number-linked OTP validation server-side

techniques.name: Race Conditions & Cache Poisoning
techniques.summary: Race the server's check-then-act windows with synchronized requests (HTTP/2 single-packet racing made this practical: 20 requests in one packet), or poison a shared cache by smuggling an unkeyed header (X-Forwarded-Host, X-Original-URL) so every subsequent user receives your payload. Web-cache poisoning is site-wide impact from a single request.

detection.description: Request-burst analytics (identical requests within one server tick), duplicate-resource errors (double-spend signatures in payment logs), cache-content drift (same URL serving different bodies to different users), header-anomaly WAF rules.
mitigations: Idempotency keys and DB unique constraints (the race's real fix)
Cache: minimize keyed-header deviations, Vary correctly, prefix cache keys with host
H2/H3 connection-window limits server-side; normalize duplicate headers
Surrogate-control discipline; cache-purge runbooks

techniques.name: Client-Side Web Attacks (XSS / CSRF / Prototype Pollution)
techniques.summary: Attacks that run in the victim's browser: stored/reflected XSS (script executes with the victim's privileges), CSRF (cross-site state-change on authenticated sessions), and DOM/prototype pollution (JS gadget chains in frameworks like jQuery/Lodash). XSS is the gateway to session theft, keylogging, and same-origin pivoting.

detection.description: DOM sandbox alerts, CSP violation reports (a real telemetry source), WAF script-tag payloads, unexpected outbound connections to user-controlled domains from browsers, account-activity anomalies following reported phishing.
mitigations: CSP with nonces (defeats inline XSS) + trusted-types for DOM sinks
Output encoding by context (HTML/attr/JS/URL) via templating engines
SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies + CSRF tokens on state-changing routes
Prototype pollution: freeze Object.prototype in sensitive apps, audit deep-merge libraries

techniques.name: Broken Access Control (IDOR / BOLA)
techniques.summary: The server asks 'does this session exist' but never 'does this session OWN this object' - so /api/invoices/1043 becomes /api/invoices/1044 and another tenant's data walks out. IDOR at object level (BOLA in the OWASP API Top 10), forced-browse at function level, parameter tampering for privilege lifts. Consistently ranked the #1 real-world web risk because it needs no payload, no injection break, no crash - just a horizontal walk an authorization layer never checked. Mostly read-class, which is why it escapes blast-radius gating while still being the quietest data breach in the catalog.

detection.description: Application logs must capture session-user AND accessed object-id, then correlate: one session touching a wide, distinct set of object ids is enumeration; canary objects (honey-records with unique ids per user) turn IDOR into a certain-signal tripwire; WSTG 4.1 authorization test matrix run in CI catches the class pre-deploy; API-gateway anomaly on 200-with-foreign-object patterns where the app logs both fields.
mitigations: Deny-by-default server-side authorization per object - never trust client-supplied object ownership
Framework-level scoping: ORM row-level filters instead of view-level checks
Per-role integration tests that assert both allow AND deny paths
Non-guessable object ids (UUIDv4+) as friction, never as the control

techniques.name: WPA/WPA2 Handshake Capture & Offline Crack
techniques.summary: Deauthenticate a client to force a 4-way handshake rekey, capture it passively, then crack the PMK-derived material offline against a wordlist (or against a stolen PMKID - deauth not even required on many APs). PSK networks with human passwords fall; enterprise networks do not (different attack surface).

detection.description: Deauth frame floods (WIDS flags them instantly), handshake capture correlation, PMKID request frames to the AP from foreign MACs; wireless IDS is the entire game here - wired monitoring sees nothing.
mitigations: WPA2-Enterprise/WPA3-SAE instead of PSK wherever humanly possible
Wireless IDS/IPS (deauth detection is standard)
Long random PSKs where PSK must remain (20+ chars, no human words)
802.11w management frame protection (makes deauth much harder)

techniques.name: Evil Twin / Rogue AP
techniques.summary: Clone a legitimate SSID on stronger signal; devices auto-associate (and auto-join wins over the real AP). Capture credentials via a cloned captive portal, strip TLS with user help, or simply MITM everything. The captive-portal phishing variant is nearly indistinguishable to untrained users.

detection.description: Same SSID from multiple BSSIDs, sudden signal-strength competition, clients authenticating twice (once to real AP, once to twin), TLS interception alerts from pinned apps, WIDS rogue-AP classification.
mitigations: Certificate validation everywhere (HSTS preload, pinned enterprise apps)
WIDS with rogue containment
Client-side: enterprise profile with CA pinning (never trust a new cert silently)
User training: verify captive portal legitimacy (look for the specific internal hostname)

techniques.name: SDR Attacks (Signal Replay / Rolling Code)
techniques.summary: Capture and replay RF signals (gate remotes, key fobs, TPMS, some alarm systems) with a $30 RTL-SDR or HackRF; fixed-code protocols replay instantly, rolling-code systems fall to predictive/capture-while-jamming. The physical world's analog of credential replay.

detection.description: Physical-layer anomalies (RF spectrum monitoring is rare outside critical facilities), unexpected unlock events in access logs, jamming complaints (the jam-then-capture signature), rolling-code sync drift (fob stops working - the user reports it).
mitigations: Rolling-code + challenge-response protocols (modern fobs); retire fixed-code devices
Faraday storage for high-value fobs where threat model warrants
RF monitoring at critical facilities
Physical access logging + anomaly review (unlock without corresponding badge event)

techniques.name: HID Injection / BadUSB-class Device Attack
techniques.summary: A USB device enumerating as HID keyboard types scripted commands in seconds (Rubber Ducky-class): open a shell, phone home, done. The host cannot distinguish it from a real keyboard by protocol; only behavioral policy catches it. Physical access plus user curiosity equals initial access.

detection.description: HID device insertion followed immediately by Win+R / terminal keystrokes (Sysmon EID 1 with new devices in EID 2001-2003 correlation), keystroke cadence inhumanly fast, devices appearing in USB history on hosts whose users report no insertion.
mitigations: USB device control policy (allowlist vendor/product, block HID where not required)
Lock screens everywhere - the attack needs an unlocked session
User awareness (unfound USB sticks are the delivery mechanism)
Endpoint hardening so one HID payload cannot chain (CLM, ASR, no auto-elevate)

_meta.eligibility: planner-visible only - NOT execution-eligible until promoted to Tier 1
_meta.promotion_rule: operator review -> author full conscience fields (detection pair, blast_radius, reversibility, requires_confirmation) -> move to techniques/*.json

records.name: Data Obfuscation
records.description: Adversaries may obfuscate command and control traffic to make it more difficult to detect.(Citation: Bitdefender FunnyDream Campaign November 2020) Command and control (C2) communications are hidden (but not necessarily encrypted) in an attempt to make the content more difficult to discover or decipher and to make the communication less conspicuous and hide commands from being seen. This encompasses many methods, such as adding junk data to protocol traffic, using steganography, or impersonating legitimate protocols.

records.name: Junk Data
records.description: Adversaries may add junk data to protocols used for command and control to make detection more difficult.(Citation: FireEye SUNBURST Backdoor December 2020) By adding random or meaningless data to the protocols used for command and control, adversaries can prevent trivial methods for decoding, deciphering, or otherwise analyzing the traffic. Examples may include appending/prepending data with junk characters or writing junk characters between significant characters.

records.name: Steganography
records.description: Adversaries may use steganographic techniques to hide command and control traffic to make detection efforts more difficult. Steganographic techniques can be used to hide data in digital messages that are transferred between systems. This hidden information can be used for command and control of compromised systems. In some cases, the passing of files embedded using steganography, such as image or document files, can be used for command and control.

records.name: Protocol or Service Impersonation
records.description:
Adversaries may impersonate legitimate protocols or web service traffic to disguise command and control activity and thwart analysis efforts. By impersonating legitimate protocols or web services, adversaries can make their command and control traffic blend in with legitimate network traffic.  

Adversaries may impersonate a fake SSL/TLS handshake to make it look like subsequent traffic is SSL/TLS encrypted, potentially interfering with some security tooling, or to make the traffic look like it is related with a trusted entity. 

Adversaries may also leverage legitimate protocols to impersonate expected web traffic or trusted services. For example, adversaries may manipulate HTTP headers, UR

records.name: OS Credential Dumping
records.description:
Adversaries may attempt to dump credentials to obtain account login and credential material, normally in the form of a hash or a clear text password. Credentials can be obtained from OS caches, memory, or structures.(Citation: Brining MimiKatz to Unix) Credentials can then be used to perform [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) and access restricted information.

Several of the tools mentioned in associated sub-techniques may be used by both adversaries and professional security testers. Additional custom tools likely exist as well.

records.name: LSASS Memory
records.description:
Adversaries may attempt to access credential material stored in the process memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS). After a user logs on, the system generates and stores a variety of credential materials in LSASS process memory. These credential materials can be harvested by an administrative user or SYSTEM and used to conduct [Lateral Movement](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0008) using [Use Alternate Authentication Material](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550).

As well as in-memory techniques, the LSASS process memory can be dumped from the target host and analyzed on a local system.

For example, on the target host use procdump:

* <code>procdump -ma

records.name: Security Account Manager
records.description: Adversaries may attempt to extract credential material from the Security Account Manager (SAM) database either through in-memory techniques or through the Windows Registry where the SAM database is stored. The SAM is a database file that contains local accounts for the host, typically those found with the net user command. Enumerating the SAM database requires SYSTEM level access. A number of tools can be used to retrieve the SAM file through in-memory techniques: * pwdumpx.exe * [gsecdump](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0008) * [Mimikatz](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0002) * secretsdump.py Alternatively, the SAM can be extracted from the Registry with Reg: *

records.name: NTDS
records.description: Adversaries may attempt to access or create a copy of the Active Directory domain database in order to steal credential information, as well as obtain other information about domain members such as devices, users, and access rights. By default, the NTDS file (NTDS.dit) is located in %SystemRoot%\NTDS\Ntds.dit of a domain controller.(Citation: Wikipedia Active Directory) In addition to looking for NTDS files on active Domain Controllers, adversaries may search for backups that contain the same or similar information.(Citation: Metcalf 2015) The following tools and techniques can be used to enumerate the NTDS file and the contents of the entire Active Directory hashes. * Volume

records.name: LSA Secrets
records.description: Adversaries with SYSTEM access to a host may attempt to access Local Security Authority (LSA) secrets, which can contain a variety of different credential materials, such as credentials for service accounts.(Citation: Passcape LSA Secrets)(Citation: Microsoft AD Admin Tier Model)(Citation: Tilbury Windows Credentials) LSA secrets are stored in the registry at HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SECURITY\Policy\Secrets. LSA secrets can also be dumped from memory.(Citation: ired Dumping LSA Secrets) [Reg](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0075) can be used to extract from the Registry. [Mimikatz](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0002) can be used to extract secrets from memory.(Citation: ired

records.name: Cached Domain Credentials
records.description:
Adversaries may attempt to access cached domain credentials used to allow authentication to occur in the event a domain controller is unavailable.(Citation: Microsoft - Cached Creds)

On Windows Vista and newer, the hash format is DCC2 (Domain Cached Credentials version 2) hash, also known as MS-Cache v2 hash.(Citation: PassLib mscache) The number of default cached credentials varies and can be altered per system. This hash does not allow pass-the-hash style attacks, and instead requires [Password Cracking](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110/002) to recover the plaintext password.(Citation: ired mscache)

On Linux systems, Active Directory credentials can be accessed through caches ma

records.name: DCSync
records.description:
Adversaries may attempt to access credentials and other sensitive information by abusing a Windows Domain Controller's application programming interface (API)(Citation: Microsoft DRSR Dec 2017) (Citation: Microsoft GetNCCChanges) (Citation: Samba DRSUAPI) (Citation: Wine API samlib.dll) to simulate the replication process from a remote domain controller using a technique called DCSync.

Members of the Administrators, Domain Admins, and Enterprise Admin groups or computer accounts on the domain controller are able to run DCSync to pull password data(Citation: ADSecurity Mimikatz DCSync) from Active Directory, which may include current and historical hashes of potentially useful accounts such

records.name: Proc Filesystem
records.description:
Adversaries may gather credentials from the proc filesystem or `/proc`. The proc filesystem is a pseudo-filesystem used as an interface to kernel data structures for Linux based systems managing virtual memory. For each process, the `/proc/<PID>/maps` file shows how memory is mapped within the process’s virtual address space. And `/proc/<PID>/mem`, exposed for debugging purposes, provides access to the process’s virtual address space.(Citation: Picus Labs Proc cump 2022)(Citation: baeldung Linux proc map 2022)

When executing with root privileges, adversaries can search these memory locations for all processes on a system that contain patterns indicative of credentials. Adversaries may use r

records.name: /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow
records.description: Adversaries may attempt to dump the contents of /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow to enable offline password cracking. Most modern Linux operating systems use a combination of /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow to store user account information, including password hashes in /etc/shadow. By default, /etc/shadow is only readable by the root user.(Citation: Linux Password and Shadow File Formats) Linux stores user information such as user ID, group ID, home directory path, and login shell in /etc/passwd. A "user" on the system may belong to a person or a service. All password hashes are stored in /etc/shadow

records.name: Data from Local System
records.description:
Adversaries may search local system sources, such as file systems, configuration files, local databases, virtual machine files, or process memory, to find files of interest and sensitive data prior to Exfiltration.

Adversaries may do this using a [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059), such as [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106) as well as a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008), which have functionality to interact with the file system to gather information.(Citation: show_run_config_cmd_cisco) Adversaries may also use [Automated Collection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1119) on the local system.

records.name: Direct Volume Access
records.description:
Adversaries may directly access a volume to bypass file access controls and file system monitoring. Windows allows programs to have direct access to logical volumes. Programs with direct access may read and write files directly from the drive by analyzing file system data structures. This technique may bypass Windows file access controls as well as file system monitoring tools.(Citation: Hakobyan 2009)

Utilities, such as `NinjaCopy`, exist to perform these actions in PowerShell.(Citation: Github PowerSploit Ninjacopy) Adversaries may also use built-in or third-party utilities (such as `vssadmin`, `wbadmin`, and [esentutl](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0404)) to create shadow copies or

records.name: System Service Discovery
records.description: Adversaries may try to gather information about registered local system services. Adversaries may obtain information about services using tools as well as OS utility commands such as sc query, tasklist /svc, systemctl --type=service, and net start. Adversaries may also gather information about schedule tasks via commands such as `schtasks` on Windows or `crontab -l` on Linux and macOS.(Citation: Elastic Security Labs GOSAR 2024)(Citation: SentinelLabs macOS Malware 2021)(Citation: Splunk Linux Gormir 2024)(Citation: Aquasec Kinsing 2020) Adversaries may use the information from [System Service Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques

records.name: Fallback Channels
records.description: Adversaries may use fallback or alternate communication channels if the primary channel is compromised or inaccessible in order to maintain reliable command and control and to avoid data transfer thresholds.

records.name: Application Window Discovery
records.description:
Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of open application windows. Window listings could convey information about how the system is used.(Citation: Prevailion DarkWatchman 2021) For example, information about application windows could be used identify potential data to collect as well as identifying security tooling ([Security Software Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1518/001)) to evade.(Citation: ESET Grandoreiro April 2020)

Adversaries typically abuse system features for this type of enumeration. For example, they may gather information through native system features such as [Command and Scripting Interpreter](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059) commands and [Nat

records.name: Exfiltration Over Other Network Medium
records.description:
Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over a different network medium than the command and control channel. If the command and control network is a wired Internet connection, the exfiltration may occur, for example, over a WiFi connection, modem, cellular data connection, Bluetooth, or another radio frequency (RF) channel.

Adversaries may choose to do this if they have sufficient access or proximity, and the connection might not be secured or defended as well as the primary Internet-connected channel because it is not routed through the same enterprise network.

records.name: Exfiltration Over Bluetooth
records.description:
Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over Bluetooth rather than the command and control channel. If the command and control network is a wired Internet connection, an adversary may opt to exfiltrate data using a Bluetooth communication channel.

Adversaries may choose to do this if they have sufficient access and proximity. Bluetooth connections might not be secured or defended as well as the primary Internet-connected channel because it is not routed through the same enterprise network.

records.name: Query Registry
records.description:
Adversaries may interact with the Windows Registry to gather information about the system, configuration, and installed software.

The Registry contains a significant amount of information about the operating system, configuration, software, and security.(Citation: Wikipedia Windows Registry) Information can easily be queried using the [Reg](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0075) utility, though other means to access the Registry exist. Some of the information may help adversaries to further their operation within a network. Adversaries may use the information from [Query Registry](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1012) during automated discovery to shape follow-on behaviors, including

records.name: Rootkit
records.description:
Adversaries may use rootkits to hide the presence of programs, files, network connections, services, drivers, and other system components. Rootkits are programs that hide the existence of malware by intercepting/hooking and modifying operating system API calls that supply system information. (Citation: Symantec Windows Rootkits) 

Rootkits or rootkit enabling functionality may reside at the user or kernel level in the operating system or lower, to include a hypervisor or [System Firmware](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1542/001). (Citation: Wikipedia Rootkit) Rootkits have been seen for Windows, Linux, and Mac OS X systems. (Citation: CrowdStrike Linux Rootkit) (Citation: BlackHat Mac

records.name: System Network Configuration Discovery
records.description:
Adversaries may look for details about the network configuration and settings, such as IP and/or MAC addresses, of systems they access or through information discovery of remote systems. Several operating system administration utilities exist that can be used to gather this information. Examples include [Arp](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0099), [ipconfig](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0100)/[ifconfig](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0101), [nbtstat](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0102), and [route](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0103).

Adversaries may also leverage a [Network Device CLI](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/008) on network devices to gather inform

records.name: Internet Connection Discovery
records.description: Adversaries may check for Internet connectivity on compromised systems. This may be performed during automated discovery and can be accomplished in numerous ways such as using [Ping](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0097), tracert, and GET requests to websites, or performing initial speed testing to confirm bandwidth. Adversaries may use the results and responses from these requests to determine if the system is capable of communicating with their C2 servers before attempting to connect to them. The results may also be used to identify routes, redirectors, and proxy servers.

records.name: Wi-Fi Discovery
records.description:
Adversaries may search for information about Wi-Fi networks, such as network names and passwords, on compromised systems. Adversaries may use Wi-Fi information as part of [Account Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1087), [Remote System Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1018), and other discovery or [Credential Access](https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0006) activity to support both ongoing and future campaigns.

Adversaries may collect various types of information about Wi-Fi networks from hosts. For example, on Windows names and passwords of all Wi-Fi networks a device has previously connected to may be available through `netsh wlan show profiles` to enumerate W

records.name: Remote System Discovery
records.description: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of other systems by IP address, hostname, or other logical identifier on a network that may be used for Lateral Movement from the current system. Functionality could exist within remote access tools to enable this, but utilities available on the operating system could also be used such as [Ping](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0097), net view using [Net](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0039), or, on ESXi servers, `esxcli network diag ping`. Adversaries may also analyze data from local host files (ex: C:\Windows\System32\Drivers\etc\hosts or /etc/hosts) or other passive means (such as local [Arp](https://a

records.name: Automated Exfiltration
records.description:
Adversaries may exfiltrate data, such as sensitive documents, through the use of automated processing after being gathered during Collection.(Citation: ESET Gamaredon June 2020) 

When automated exfiltration is used, other exfiltration techniques likely apply as well to transfer the information out of the network, such as [Exfiltration Over C2 Channel](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1041) and [Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1048).

records.name: Traffic Duplication
records.description:
Adversaries may leverage traffic mirroring in order to automate data exfiltration over compromised infrastructure. Traffic mirroring is a native feature for some devices, often used for network analysis. For example, devices may be configured to forward network traffic to one or more destinations for analysis by a network analyzer or other monitoring device. (Citation: Cisco Traffic Mirroring)(Citation: Juniper Traffic Mirroring)

Adversaries may abuse traffic mirroring to mirror or redirect network traffic through other infrastructure they control. Malicious modifications to network devices to enable traffic redirection may be possible through [ROMMONkit](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques

records.name: Remote Services
records.description:
Adversaries may use [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to log into a service that accepts remote connections, such as telnet, SSH, and VNC. The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

In an enterprise environment, servers and workstations can be organized into domains. Domains provide centralized identity management, allowing users to login using one set of credentials across the entire network. If an adversary is able to obtain a set of valid domain credentials, they could login to many different machines using remote access protocols such as secure shell (SSH) or remote desktop protocol (RDP).(Citation: SSH Secure Shell)(Citation: TechNet Remote

records.name: Remote Desktop Protocol
records.description:
Adversaries may use [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to log into a computer using the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

Remote desktop is a common feature in operating systems. It allows a user to log into an interactive session with a system desktop graphical user interface on a remote system. Microsoft refers to its implementation of the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) as Remote Desktop Services (RDS).(Citation: TechNet Remote Desktop Services) 

Adversaries may connect to a remote system over RDP/RDS to expand access if the service is enabled and allows access to accounts with known credentials. Adversari

records.name: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
records.description:
Adversaries may use [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to interact with a remote network share using Server Message Block (SMB). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

SMB is a file, printer, and serial port sharing protocol for Windows machines on the same network or domain. Adversaries may use SMB to interact with file shares, allowing them to move laterally throughout a network. Linux and macOS implementations of SMB typically use Samba.

Windows systems have hidden network shares that are accessible only to administrators and provide the ability for remote file copy and other administrative functions. Example network shares include `C$`, `

records.name: Distributed Component Object Model
records.description:
Adversaries may use [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to interact with remote machines by taking advantage of Distributed Component Object Model (DCOM). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

The Windows Component Object Model (COM) is a component of the native Windows application programming interface (API) that enables interaction between software objects, or executable code that implements one or more interfaces. Through COM, a client object can call methods of server objects, which are typically Dynamic Link Libraries (DLL) or executables (EXE). Distributed COM (DCOM) is transparent middleware that extends the functionality of COM beyond

records.name: SSH
records.description:
Adversaries may use [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to log into remote machines using Secure Shell (SSH). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

SSH is a protocol that allows authorized users to open remote shells on other computers. Many Linux and macOS versions come with SSH installed by default, although typically disabled until the user enables it. On ESXi, SSH can be enabled either directly on the host (e.g., via `vim-cmd hostsvc/enable_ssh`) or via vCenter.(Citation: Sygnia ESXi Ransomware 2025)(Citation: TrendMicro ESXI Ransomware)(Citation: Sygnia Abyss Locker 2025) The SSH server can be configured to use standard password authentic

records.name: VNC
records.description:
Adversaries may use [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to remotely control machines using Virtual Network Computing (VNC).  VNC is a platform-independent desktop sharing system that uses the RFB (“remote framebuffer”) protocol to enable users to remotely control another computer’s display by relaying the screen, mouse, and keyboard inputs over the network.(Citation: The Remote Framebuffer Protocol)

VNC differs from [Remote Desktop Protocol](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/001) as VNC is screen-sharing software rather than resource-sharing software. By default, VNC uses the system's authentication, but it can be configured to use credentials specific to VNC

records.name: Windows Remote Management
records.description:
Adversaries may use [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to interact with remote systems using Windows Remote Management (WinRM). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

WinRM is the name of both a Windows service and a protocol that allows a user to interact with a remote system (e.g., run an executable, modify the Registry, modify services).(Citation: Microsoft WinRM) It may be called with the `winrm` command or by any number of programs such as PowerShell.(Citation: Jacobsen 2014) WinRM  can be used as a method of remotely interacting with [Windows Management Instrumentation](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1047).(Citation: MSDN WMI)

records.name: Cloud Services
records.description:
Adversaries may log into accessible cloud services within a compromised environment using [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) that are synchronized with or federated to on-premises user identities. The adversary may then perform management actions or access cloud-hosted resources as the logged-on user. 

Many enterprises federate centrally managed user identities to cloud services, allowing users to login with their domain credentials in order to access the cloud control plane. Similarly, adversaries may connect to available cloud services through the web console or through the cloud command line interface (CLI) (e.g., [Cloud API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T

records.name: Direct Cloud VM Connections
records.description:
Adversaries may leverage [Valid Accounts](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078) to log directly into accessible cloud hosted compute infrastructure through cloud native methods. Many cloud providers offer interactive connections to virtual infrastructure that can be accessed through the [Cloud API](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/009), such as Azure Serial Console(Citation: Azure Serial Console), AWS EC2 Instance Connect(Citation: EC2 Instance Connect)(Citation: lucr-3: Getting SaaS-y in the cloud), and AWS System Manager.(Citation: AWS System Manager).

Methods of authentication for these connections can include passwords, application access tokens, or SSH keys. These cloud n

records.name: Data from Removable Media
records.description:
Adversaries may search connected removable media on computers they have compromised to find files of interest. Sensitive data can be collected from any removable media (optical disk drive, USB memory, etc.) connected to the compromised system prior to Exfiltration. Interactive command shells may be in use, and common functionality within [cmd](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0106) may be used to gather information. 

Some adversaries may also use [Automated Collection](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1119) on removable media.

records.name: Multiband Communication
records.description:
**This technique has been deprecated and should no longer be used.**

Some adversaries may split communications between different protocols. There could be one protocol for inbound command and control and another for outbound data, allowing it to bypass certain firewall restrictions. The split could also be random to simply avoid data threshold alerts on any one communication.

records.name: Obfuscated Files or Information
records.description:
Adversaries may attempt to make an executable or file difficult to discover or analyze by encrypting, encoding, or otherwise obfuscating its contents on the system or in transit. This is common behavior that can be used across different platforms and the network to evade defenses. 

Payloads may be compressed, archived, or encrypted in order to avoid detection. These payloads may be used during Initial Access or later to mitigate detection. Sometimes a user's action may be required to open and [Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1140) for [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204). The user may also be required to input a password t

records.name: Binary Padding
records.description:
Adversaries may use binary padding to add junk data and change the on-disk representation of malware. This can be done without affecting the functionality or behavior of a binary, but can increase the size of the binary beyond what some security tools are capable of handling due to file size limitations. 

Binary padding effectively changes the checksum of the file and can also be used to avoid hash-based blocklists and static anti-virus signatures.(Citation: ESET OceanLotus) The padding used is commonly generated by a function to create junk data and then appended to the end or applied to sections of malware.(Citation: Securelist Malware Tricks April 2017) Increasing the file size may decre

records.name: Software Packing
records.description:
Adversaries may perform software packing or virtual machine software protection to conceal their code. Software packing is a method of compressing or encrypting an executable. Packing an executable changes the file signature in an attempt to avoid signature-based detection. Most decompression techniques decompress the executable code in memory. Virtual machine software protection translates an executable's original code into a special format that only a special virtual machine can run. A virtual machine is then called to run this code.(Citation: ESET FinFisher Jan 2018) 

Utilities used to perform software packing are called packers. Example packers are MPRESS and UPX. A more comprehensive l

records.name: Steganography
records.description: Adversaries may use steganography techniques in order to prevent the detection of hidden information. Steganographic techniques can be used to hide data in digital media such as images, audio tracks, video clips, or text files. [Duqu](https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0038) was an early example of malware that used steganography. It encrypted the gathered information from a victim's system and hid it within an image before exfiltrating the image to a C2 server.(Citation: Wikipedia Duqu) By the end of 2017, a threat group used Invoke-PSImage to hide [PowerShell](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001) commands in an image file (.png) and execute the code on a victim's

records.name: Compile After Delivery
records.description:
Adversaries may attempt to make payloads difficult to discover and analyze by delivering files to victims as uncompiled code. Text-based source code files may subvert analysis and scrutiny from protections targeting executables/binaries. These payloads will need to be compiled before execution; typically via native utilities such as ilasm.exe(Citation: ATTACK IQ), csc.exe, or GCC/MinGW.(Citation: ClearSky MuddyWater Nov 2018)

Source code payloads may also be encrypted, encoded, and/or embedded within other files, such as those delivered as a [Phishing](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566). Payloads may also be delivered in formats unrecognizable and inherently benign to the native OS

records.name: Indicator Removal from Tools
records.description:
Adversaries may remove indicators from tools if they believe their malicious tool was detected, quarantined, or otherwise curtailed.
